Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verses 1–2:

Meccan, and it has one hundred and nineteen verses; the Kufans count eighteen [it was revealed after Surat al-Anbiya']. In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

"Qad" is the counterpart of "lamma": "qad" affirms what is expected, while "lamma" negates it. There is no doubt that the believers were expecting such good news, which is the announcement that success is firmly theirs, so they were addressed with words indicating the confirmation of what they had hoped for. And "al-falah" (success):

It is attaining the desired goal. It has also been said: remaining in goodness. "Aflaha" means he entered into success, like "abshara," meaning he entered into good news.

It is said: "aflahahu" means he caused him to reach success. Upon this is the reading of Talha ibn Musarrif: "uflih," in the passive form.

And from him: "aflahu" (with a plural verb), as in the phrase "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me), or on the basis of an undefined subject explained afterwards. And from him: "aflah," with a single damma without the waw, the damma standing in for it, as in the poet's words:

"Had the physicians been around me, and the healers were with the physicians..."

The original is "kanu hawli" (they were around me); he shortened it, and shortened "al-atibba'" (the physicians) for the sake of the metre. They are the scholars of medicine. "Al-asah" is the plural of "asin," like "al-su'ah" is the plural of "sa'in," and they are those who directly carry out treatment among the physicians, from "al-asa" (healing) like "al-fata," meaning treatment. "Al-isa'" with a kasra is medicine, and perhaps this is the origin of the narration, just as the narration reads "al-shifa'," so its proper form carries the letter alif.

If you ask: what is the "mu'min"? I answer: linguistically it is the one who affirms the truth. In the Shari'ah, however, it has been disputed on two views. One: that everyone who utters the two testimonies with his heart in agreement with his tongue is a believer. The other: that it is a term of praise which is deserved only by the righteous and pious, not by the wicked and miserable sinner. [Mahmud said: "There is disagreement about faith on two views: one, that everyone who utters the two testimonies with his heart in agreement with his tongue has attained faith; the other, that it is a term of praise deserved only by the righteous and pious, not the wicked and miserable sinner." Ahmad said: the first is the position of the Ash'aris, and the second is the position of the Mu'tazilah. The unitarian sinner, according to them, is neither a believer nor an unbeliever. Had the Mu'tazilah not built on this belief the prohibition of Paradise for the unitarian sinner, on the basis that he is not included in the promise to the believers, the dispute with them would be merely verbal; but they constructed upon it a great matter from the foundations and principles of religion. The judge (al-Qadi) has transmitted from them in the Risalat al-Iman a lengthy confusion: he transmitted from their early figures such as 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and his circle that faith is the affirmation of the heart together with all the obligations of religion, in both action and abstention. And it is transmitted from Abu al-Hudhayl al-'Allaf that faith is all the obligations and supererogatory acts of religion. The summary of the judge's argument against the People of the Sunnah is that faith linguistically is merely affirmation, by agreement, so it must be so in the Shari'ah, in accordance with the words of the Exalted: "We did not send any messenger except in the tongue of his people," together with its freedom from contradiction by transmission, for had it been different for His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and had he explained it, it would have been transmitted, because it is among the matters upon which the rule of promise and threat is built; and it was not transmitted, since transmission is either solitary (ahad) or mass-transmitted (tawatur)... to the end of its material.]] Humility in prayer (khushu') is the fear of the heart and the lowering of the gaze. From Qatadah: it is making his gaze fixed on the place of prostration.

And from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he used to pray raising his gaze to the sky; when this verse was revealed he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration. [Al-Hakim transmitted it from the narration of Ibn Sirin from Abu Hurayrah, but he said "he lowered his head," and declared it sound, except that it was transmitted as mursal (with a missing companion). The mursal version was transmitted by Abu Dawud and al-Tabari from Ibn Sirin from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and he said: "in it there is consideration, thus." It was also transmitted by al-Wahidi in al-Asbab through the route of Ibn 'Ulayyah, from Ayyub, from Ibn Sirin, connected (mawsul).] And a man of the scholars, when he stood for prayer, would be in awe of the Merciful, so as not to fix his gaze on anything, or to occupy his mind with some matter of worldly affairs. It was also said: it is gathering one's resolve toward it and turning away from all else. Among humility is observing the proper etiquette: avoiding rolling up one's sleeves, playing with one's body and clothing, turning the head, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, wrapping oneself (sadl), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, shortening the prayer, and moving pebbles. It is related from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he saw a man fiddling with his beard during prayer and said: "If his heart were humbled, his limbs would be humbled." [Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted it in al-Nawadir, in the forty-sixth after the hundredth, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and in its chain is Sulayman ibn 'Amr, who is Abu Dawud al-Nakha'i, one of those accused of fabricating hadith. In Zayn al-Din ibn al-Munir's commentary on al-Bukhari, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said to 'A'ishah: "If the heart of this one were humbled, his limbs would be humbled."] Al-Hasan saw a man playing with pebbles while saying: "O Allah, marry me to the wide-eyed houris," so he said: "What a wretched suitor you are! You propose while you are playing." If you ask: why is the prayer attributed to them? I answer: because the prayer revolves between the one who prays and the one to whom it is prayed. The one who prays is the one who alone benefits from it, and it is his provision and treasure, so it is his prayer. As for the One to whom it is prayed, He is self-sufficient and exalted above any need for it or benefit from it.

Zakah is a homonym for a thing and a meaning. The thing is the portion that the one paying zakah (al-muzakki) gives from the minimum amount (nisab) to the poor. The meaning is the action of the one paying zakah, which is the purifying (al-tazkiyah), and this is what God intended. So He made those who pay zakah the doers of it (fa'ilun lahu), and nothing else is appropriate here, because every verbal noun (masdar) expresses its meaning through a verb, and the one who brings it about is called its doer. You say of one who strikes, "the doer of striking" (fa'il al-darb), and of one who kills, "the doer of killing" (fa'il al-qatl), and of one who pays zakah, "the doer of purifying" (fa'il al-tazkiyah). On all of this, and the verification of it, you say about every event: "Who is the doer of this?" and you are told: "Its doer is God, or some of the creatures."

[[Mahmud said: "Zakah is used to mean the thing given out, and it is used to mean the action of the one paying it, which is purifying. Here it is necessarily the purifying, because of His saying ﴿those who are doers of it﴾, since the thing given out was not done by the one paying it. Then he defined the verbal noun absolutely as that of which it is truly said that it is the act of the agent. On this basis, the thing given out is a verbal noun in relation to God Most High, and likewise the heavens and the earth and every created thing of substance or accident. He said: so for all events, if it is asked who is their doer, it is said: God, or some of the creatures." Ahmad said: The Sunni says: the doer of all of them is God alone, without partner. But if he is asked with a form derived from the verb in the manner of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), such as being asked, "Who is standing? Who is sitting?", he answers: the one upon whose hands God created the act and made him its locus, like Zayd and 'Amr.]]

The word zakah, which denotes the thing, does not prevent the verb "doers" (fa'ilun) from being connected to it, because it is an object that can be taken by the doer. Rather, creatures are not its doers. And the poet Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt has said:

"Those who feed the food in the year of dearth, and those who are doers of the zakat-payments."

[[Of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt. Al-azm means drought, and al-azmah is the severe, barren year. Al-zakawat is the plural of zakah, which is used for the amount given out from property and for the giving out. So the meaning on the first use is: those who discharge the zakat-payments. On the second: those who do that giving out. The first is more apt, because the verbal noun is pluralized only by considering kinds or occasions.]] It is also permissible that zakah means the thing, with an omitted genitive-governed noun (mudaf mahdhuf) estimated, which is "the discharging" (al-ada'). Taking the line in this sense is more correct, because the word is in plural there.

Upon their spouses (ʿalā azwājihim) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: those who are constant (al-awwālīn) with respect to their spouses. Or it means: those who are in charge of them (qawwāmīn ʿalayhinna), from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so," (kāna fulān ʿalā fulāna), then he died leaving her, and so-and-so succeeded to her (fa-khallafa ʿalayhā fulān). Its parallel is: "Ziyād was over Basra" (kāna Ziyād ʿalā al-Baṣra), meaning: he was governor over it (wāliyan ʿalayhā). From this is their saying: "So-and-so is under so-and-so" (fulāna taḥta fulān). It is from this that the woman was called a bed (firāsh).

The meaning is: they guard their private parts in all circumstances, except in the case of marrying them or taking them as concubines (tasarrīhim). Or ʿalā is connected to a deleted element that is indicated by ghayru malūmīn, as though it were said: they are blamed, except regarding their spouses; that is, they are blamed for every sexual partner except for what has been permitted to them, for they are not blamed for that.

Or you may make it a complement to ḥāfiẓūn (guarding), from your saying: "Guard for me the reins of my horse" (uḥfaẓ ʿalayya ʿinān farasī), with it being construed to contain the meaning of negation, just as their saying "I adjure you by God except you do such-and-such" (nashadtuka billāh illā faʿalta) is construed to contain the meaning of "what I asked of you is nothing but your doing."

If you say: why was it not said "those whom your right hands possess" (man malakat)? I say: because what is intended is a class of rational beings, and what is treated like non-rational beings, namely females. The exception was made a limit at which one must stop. Then He said: whoever seeks beyond this limit, despite its breadth and expansiveness, which is the permission of four free women and whatever concubines you wish, then those are the ones who are the complete transgressors (al-kāmilūn fī al-ʿudwān), those who go to the furthest extreme in it.

If you say: is there in this evidence for the prohibition of temporary marriage (mutʿa)? I say: no, because a woman in a temporary marriage is among the spouses (azwāj), provided the marriage is valid.

Also read: li-amanatihim (their trusts). The thing entrusted and the thing pledged is called "amana" (trust) and "ahd" (covenant). From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [4:58], and He said: ﴿and do not betray your trusts﴾ [8:27]. Only the eyes render (tu'addi) [something], not the meanings, and it is the one entrusted who is betrayed (yukhan), not the trust itself. And "ra'i" (the one who shepherds): the one who stands over a thing with preservation and upkeep, like the shepherd of sheep and the shepherd of a people. It is said: "Who is the ra'i of this thing?" meaning, its custodian and owner. It may be general, covering everything they were entrusted with and bound to, both from Allah the Exalted and from creation, and it may be specific to what they bore of people's trusts and covenants.

It is also read ʿalā ṣalawātihim (in the plural, "upon their prayers"). If you ask: how is the mention of prayer repeated, first and last? I answer: these are two different mentions, so it is not mere repetition. They are described first as having humility (khushūʿ) in their prayer, and last as guarding (muḥāfaẓah) it. That means they do not neglect it, perform it at its times, observe its pillars (arkān), and bind themselves to attend to it and to what its attributes must be completed with. Also, it is stated in the singular first in order to convey humility in the category of prayer, whatever prayer it is, and it is stated in the plural last in order to convey the guarding of its numbers: these are the five daily prayers, the witr, the regular sunnah prayers attached to each prayer, the Friday prayer, the two ʿEid prayers, the funeral prayer, the prayer for rain (istisqāʾ), the eclipse prayers (kusūf and khusūf), the forenoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā), the night prayer (tahajjud), the prayer of glorification (ṣalāt al-tasbīḥ), the prayer of need (ṣalāt al-ḥājah), and other supererogatory prayers (nawāfil).

Thus those who combine these attributes are the true inheritors, deserving to be called inheritors above all others. Then He specified the inheritors with His words: "who shall inherit al-Firdaws," which came with a grandeur and eloquence in the inheritance that is not hidden from the observer. The meaning of inheritance is what has passed in Surah Maryam. The word al-Firdaws is feminine in agreement with its interpretation as al-Jannah (the Garden), and it is: the wide orchard comprising all kinds of fruit. It is related that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, built the Garden of al-Firdaws with a brick of gold and a brick of silver, and placed between them musk of the finest quality (al-miskh al-adhfar). And in another narration: "and a brick of pure musk (misk mudharra), and He planted in it the finest fruit and the finest fragrant herbs (rayhan)."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verse 12–14:

As-sulalah: the best part (al-khulasah), because it is drawn out (tusall) from among the turbidity (al-kadar). The form fi'alah is a pattern for diminution, as in qalamah (parings of nails) and qamamah (sweepings). It is reported from al-Hasan: water between the surfaces of the clay.

If you say: What is the difference between min and min? I say: the first is for the beginning (ibtida', the starting point), and the second is for explanation (bayan), as in His words ﴿mina l-awthan﴾ (﴿from the idols﴾).

If you say: What is the meaning of ﴿Then We placed him as a drop of seed (nutfah)﴾? I say:

Its meaning is that He first created the essence of the human being as clay, then after that made his essence a drop of seed. Al-qarar: the place of settling, and what is meant is the womb. It is described with the place-quality, which is the attribute of the one who settles in it, as in your saying "a traveling road" (tariq sa'ir). Or by the place-quality of itself, because it is firm and secured in what it is.

It was read: ﴿'izaman fa-kasawna l-'izam﴾, and ﴿'izaman fa-kasawna l-'izam﴾ and ﴿'izaman fa-kasawna l-'izam﴾. The singular is placed in the position of the plural to remove ambiguity, since the human being has many bones. ﴿Khalqan akhar﴾ means a creation distinct from the first creation, with a distinction of what a distance it is, since He made him an animal when he was inanimate, speaking when he was mute, hearing when he was deaf, seeing when he was blind, and deposited in his inner and outer parts, indeed in every organ of his and every part of his parts, wonders of natural design and strange wisdom that cannot be grasped by the description of any describer nor reached by the explanation of any explainer. Abu Hanifah argued from this concerning one who usurped an egg which then hatched in his possession: he said he must pay for the egg and does not return the chick, because it is a creation other than the egg.

Ibn Abi Abla and Ibn Muhaysin read: لمائتون (lamā'itūn). The difference between al-mayyit (the dead, one who is dead) and al-ma'it (one who is dying/about to die) is that al-mayyit, like al-hayy (the living), denotes a fixed, enduring attribute. As for al-ma'it, it denotes occurrence and newness. You say: "Zayd is dying now (ma'it al-an), and dying tomorrow (ma'it ghadan)," just as you say yamutu (he dies). Similar to them are: ḍayyiq and ḍā'iq, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَضَائِقٌ بِهِ صَدْرُكَ﴾ ("and your breast is constricted by it").

He made the causing of death, which is the annihilation of life, and the resurrection, which is the restoration of what He brings to an end and annihilates, two further proofs of great power after the bringing into existence and the originating. If you say: then there is no life except the life of origination and the life of resurrection. with measure (بِقَدَرٍ): that is, by a determination through which they are safe from harm and attain benefit. *"I saw those in need around their dwellings,

*"If the white year afflicts the people
and the noble among them obtain food only in the lean season,"*

*"There, if they are asked for wealth, they give it;

It is also reported as *kirām al-māl* (noble wealth). The meaning is that the noble wealth was reached by consumption and depletion in that year because of its scarcity.

It is said: *yasara* (like *waʿada*) means to play the maysir; and *yasura* (like *taraba* and *taʿiba*) means to be easy and gentle. It is reported as:

*"yas'alū wa yayassarū"* in the present tense.

*Al-maqāmāt* means the gatherings of people. It is reported as *wujūhuhā* (its faces). In either case the pronoun refers to *al-maqāmāt*.

*Al-andiya*, the plural of *al-nadā*, means generosity, contrary to the regular pattern. *Yantābuhā*: that is, there is recurring, turn after turn, of their speech and their deeds upon them. Or the speech of people and their deeds circulate around them. It is possible that it is the plural of *nādin*, meaning the speaker of a people, or *nadan* in the form *faʿīl* in the same sense. *Yantābuhā*: that is, there comes to them, turn after turn, speech and deeds, that is, the good ones.

The second possibility: its object is omitted, meaning: it grows its olives, and in it is oil. It has been read as *tunbitu* with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and a fatḥa on the bāʾ, and its ruling is the same as *tunbitu* (the previous reading). Ibn Masʿūd read: *tukhriju al-duhn wa ṣibgh lil-ākilīn*. Others read: *takhruju bil-duhn*. In the variant of Ubayy: *tuthmiru bil-duhn*. It is reported from some of them: *tunbitu bil-dahhān*. Al-Aʿmash read: *wa ṣabghan*, and it has been read *wa ṣibāgh*. Similar to them: *dabgh* and *dibāgh*. *Al-ṣabgh* is dipping for seasoning. It has been said that it is the first tree that grew after the Flood, and God Most High described it with blessing in His words: ﴿يُوقَدُ مِنْ شَجَرَةٍ مُبارَكَةٍ﴾ ("It is lit from a blessed tree," Q 24:35).

It is read as **tusqīkum** (تسقيكم), with an open *tā’*, meaning: "the cattle give you to drink." **وَمِنْها تَأْكُلُونَ** ﴿and from them you eat﴾: there are benefits in them from riding, carrying and other uses, just as there are benefits in those animals whose meat is not eaten, such as horses, mules and donkeys. There is also an additional benefit, which is eating, that is, benefiting from their very substance. By "the cattle" he means camels, because they are the animals normally used for carrying loads. He joins them with **الفلك** (al-fulk, "the ships") because camels are the "ships of the desert" (*safā'in barr*).

Dhū al-Rummah said:

*Did Mayya visit me in a dream, when my companions were asleep? Only her greeting drove away my drowsiness.*

*She came at night, and the saddle-frame was fastened to a ship of the desert whose rein lay under my cheek.*

*She knelt down and threw off a hard ground upon hard ground, where few sounds were heard except her bellowing.*

Dhū al-Rummah means: "Mayya appeared to me in a vision, showed me her image, and greeted me in my sleep, while my companions slept." The word **صحبة** (ṣuḥbah, "companions") is like **عصبة** (ʿuṣbah, "group") and **رفقة** (rufqah, "company"). He attributes the sleep to them and not to himself, because his sleep was only **التهويم** (al-tahwīm, "dozing"), meaning a slackening and inattentiveness at the very beginning of sleep. **التهويم** also means the swaying of the head from drowsiness. Alternatively, he remembers her, so it is as if he had not slept.

It is also narrated as: **ذو الكرى** (dhū al-karā, "the one who is awake") instead of **صحبتي**, meaning: "Only her greeting drove away the drowsiness from me." It is also narrated as:

*Mayya, daughter of Munthir, visited us at night, and only her greeting kept the sleepers awake.*

**أرّق** means "kept awake," and **النيام** is the plural of **نائم** (nāʾim, "sleeper"). Its regular plural would be **نوام**, but the *yāʾ* has been changed to a *wāw* irregularly. **الطروق** means coming at night. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of **خيلت** ("showed her image"), since the two share the same meaning. It is said that **الطروق** with a *fatḥah* means a she-camel that has reached the age when the stallion mounts her; in that case it is the object of **خيلت**. The more probable reading is that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of the verb. This may be a figurative comparison.

**جلب الرحل** (jalab al-raḥl, "the frame of the saddle") with a *ḍammah* or a *kasrah* means its wooden framework. That is, the wooden frame of the saddle was fastened to a large she-camel, like a ship. He used the metaphor explicitly, and the addition "of the desert" (**برّ**) is the clue to the metaphor. In it there is the indication that in the desert she takes the place of a ship at sea, and corresponds to it. **الزمام** (al-zimām, "the rein") is an abstraction (*tajrīd*): her rein was under my cheek while I was sleeping.

**البلدة** (al-baldah) of a camel is the part that touches the ground when she kneels, and it is also used for her chest. **البلدة** also means hard ground. **البغام** (al-bughām) is the cry of a gazelle. That is: "I made her kneel, and she threw down hard bones like the ground, upon hard ground, where there were few sounds except the camel's cry, that is, her sound resembling a gazelle's, because it was a yearning moan." The use of a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun without delay, negation or restriction is irregular (*shādh*). It is also narrated as **قليل** (qalīl) in the genitive, as an attribute. In either case, **الأصوات** is the subject of the clause, and the exception is in the nominative by *ittibāʿ* (agreement with the preceding word), because **قليلا** has the sense of negation. That is: there was no sound except the cry. It is also said that **إلا** here means **غير** ("other than"), so it is an attribute of **الأصوات**, since it resembles an indefinite noun. When the case-ending could not appear on it, it appeared on the word following it.

Ghayruhu is read in the nominative on the basis of location (maḥall), and in the genitive on the basis of the wording (lafẓ). The clause is a resumed statement (istiʾnāf) that functions as a justification (taʿlīl) for the command to worship: أَفَلا تَتَّقُونَ "Will you not then be mindful of God?" That is: will you not fear abandoning the worship of God, who is your Lord, your Creator and your Provider, while the thanks due for His blessings, which you cannot count, is an obligation upon you, and then go on to worship other than Him, which has no claim whatsoever to worship? أَنْ يَتَفَضَّلَ عَلَيْكُمْ "that he may seek superiority over you and lead you," as in His saying, Exalted is He: وَتَكُونَ لَكُمَا الْكِبْرِياءُ فِي الْأَرْضِ "and that greatness in the land may be yours" (Q. 10:78). بِهذا "by this" refers to Noah, peace be upon him, or to what they were told of the exhortation to worship God. That is: we have not heard of the like of this speech, or of the like of this man who claims, though he is a human being, that he is the Messenger of God. How strange is the state of misguidance: they would not accept a human being for prophethood, yet they accepted a stone for divinity!

Their saying مَا سَمِعْنا بِهذا "We have not heard of this" indicates that they and their fathers were in a lengthy interval (fatrah) without a messenger. Or they lied in this regard, due to their immersion in error and their eagerness to repel the truth by whatever means were available to them and whatever occurred to them, without any discrimination between truth and falsehood. Do you not see how they called him a madman, though they knew that he was the most intelligent of people and the most sound in speech?

al-Janna (الجنة) means madness or the jinn, i.e., "there is in him a jinn who afflicts him" (Arabic: بِهِ جِنَّةٌ). حَتَّى حِينٍ "until a time": bear with him and be patient with him until a period of time, until his affair becomes clear with a result; if he recovers from his madness, well and good; otherwise, you may kill him.

It is related that it was said to Noah, peace be upon him: "When you see the water gushing forth from the tannur (oven), then board the ship, you and those with you." So when the water burst forth from the tannur, his wife informed him, and he boarded. It was also said that the tannur was Adam's, peace be upon him, and that it was made of stone, and it passed to Noah.

They differed about its location. From al-Shaʿbi: in the Mosque of Kufa, on the right of the one entering from the side of the Kinda Gate, and Noah had built the ship in the middle of the mosque. It was also said: in al-Sham, at a place called ʿAyn Warda. It was also said: in India.

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: the tannur is the surface of the earth. From Qatada: the most elevated place on earth, that is, its highest part. From ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "The tannur gushed" means the dawn broke. It was also said: its meaning is that the gushing of the tannur was at the dawn's lighting up. It was also said: it is a figure of speech, like their saying, "The furnace has become hot (ḥamiya al-waṭīs)." The first opinion is the correct one.

It is said: "Salaka fīhi" means he entered it, and "salaka ghayrahu" and "aslakahu" (both mean he made someone enter). A poet said:

*Until, when they drove them into its narrow passes,*
*They were driven like a herd of scattered camels.*

It is by ʿAbd Manaf ibn Rabiʿ al-Hudhali, describing a people who were raided: they repelled the enemy until they drove them into its narrow passes. Qatāʾid is a specific mountain pass, or a specific steep path, that is, in its routes. "Salakahu fī kadhā" and "aslakahu" likewise, as here, mean: he made him enter it. It is also related as "salakūhum" (without the alif). "Shalan" means being driven away, and it is in the accusative as the object of their driving, because it carries the sense of "they drove them." "Idhā" is a superfluous particle with no answer, since the verse is the last of the poem, as is stated in al-Sihah. It was also said that "shalan" is its answer, and it is then in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: they were confined in a confinement. But this does not suit the simile in "as the herd is driven," unless it refers back to their driving. "Al-jamāla" is the plural of jammāl, the herder of camels. "Al-sharad" (with two fatḥas) means scattered camels, or (with two ḍammas) the plural of sharūd, like ʿarūs.

﴿Of every pair, two﴾: of every community, a pair, namely the male community and the female community, like the camels and she-camels, and the stallions and mares. ﴿Two﴾: singly, each being one of a pair, like the male camel and the she-camel, and the stallion and the mare. It is related that he carried only what gives birth and lays eggs. It is also read as "min kullin" with tanwīn, meaning: from every community, a pair. "Ithnayn" is for emphasis and additional clarification.

﴿ʿAlā﴾ is used with harm, as ﴿lām﴾ is used with benefit. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾, and ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾, and similar to it His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and it has what it acquired﴾. And ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I wish it had been equal, neither against me nor for me."

If you ask: Why did He forbid him from praying for their deliverance? I say: because of what the verse implies, that they are wrongdoers, and wisdom requires that they must be drowned without doubt, since the benefit in drowning them and the harm in sparing them is known. After Allah had given them a long respite, and they only increased in misguidance, and the decisive proof was established against them, nothing remained except to make them a lesson for those who take heed. He has emphasized this greatly: He followed the prohibition with the command to praise Him for their destruction and for the deliverance from them, as in His saying: ﴿So the last remnant of the wrongdoing people was cut off, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Then He commanded him to supplicate with a supplication that is more important and more beneficial for him, namely asking Allah to make him land in the ship or on the earth when he disembarks from it, at a place that is blessed for him and in which He gives him increase in the good of both abodes. And He commanded him to conclude the supplication with praise of Allah that matches his request, which is His saying: ﴿And You are the best of those who bring to land﴾.

If you ask: Why was it not said, "Then say," in accordance with His saying: ﴿When you have settled, you and those with you﴾, since it has the sense of "When you (plural) have settled"? I say: because he is their prophet and their leader, so his saying is their saying, along with what it implies of the excellence of prophethood and the display of the majesty of lordship, and that the rank of such an address is not attained except by an angel or a prophet.

It is also read as "munzalan" (with fatḥa on the zāy), meaning "inzālan" (the act of bringing down), or "place of descent," like His saying: ﴿He will certainly admit them to an admission they will be pleased with﴾.

﴿Indeed﴾ here is the light form of the heavy one, and the lām is the one that distinguishes it from the negative in meaning. The affair and the matter is: ﴿We were indeed testing﴾, that is, We were striking the people of Noah with a great affliction and severe punishment.

*Al-Kashshaf* of al-Zamakhshari, on surah 23, verses 31–32:

"Another generation" (*qarnan akharina*): they are the people of 'Ad, the people of Hud. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is supported by Allah's recounting of Hud's words: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh﴾, and by the placement of the story of Hud directly after the story of Nuh in Surat al-A'raf, Surat Hud and Surat al-Shu'ara'.

If you ask: the proper construction of *arsala* ("to send") is that it takes *ila* ("to"), like its sisters *wajjaha* ("to direct"), *anfadha* ("to dispatch") and *ba'atha* ("to send forth"). Why, then, is it followed by *ila* in some places in the Qur'an, while in others it is left without it, as in His saying: ﴿Thus We sent you to a community, and We did not send any warner into a town, except...﴾, and ﴿So We sent among them a messenger﴾, meaning among 'Ad; and in another place ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud﴾?

I answer: it was not given *bi-* (in) the way it was given *ila* (to), nor was it treated as a complement of the same kind. Rather, the community or the town was made the place of the sending, as Ru'ba said:

*"I sent into it a bold, impetuous stallion,*
*Skilled and knowing with the she-camels that are in heat."*

The verse is in *al-Ta'ayish* or similar. It is said: "the camel became *musa'ab* (untamed)" when it became too wild to be ridden. *Al-iqham* means entering into a matter without delay or deliberation. It is also transmitted as: *"I sent into it a stirred-up, eager male, possessing the scent (of the she-camels)"*. *Aqramtuhu* means I aroused him to mate. Similar is *dhu tashammum*, meaning he sniffs the scent of the she-camel that is eager for mating and recognises it. *Al-tabb* (with the vowel variants) is the skilled physician. *Ablamat al-naqatu iblaman* means the vulva of the she-camel swelled from the intensity of her desire for mating. *Al-balm* (on the pattern of *sabab*) is its noun. It is permissible that *ma huna* here is *ablam* (on the pattern of *asbab*). The meaning is then: he was sent among the camels as a noble stallion who approaches them without hesitation, or who sniffs them and identifies them, being skilled and knowing of the she-camels that long for him. It is also permissible that the meaning is: in that affair I sent a man like a powerful camel, bold in acting upon the matter with courage, a jurist who knows how to deal with difficult things that have obstacles, and how to resolve their problems; he is at the utmost level of knowledge and experience.

The word *ba'atha* has come with this meaning in His saying: ﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner into every town﴾.

*An* here is explanatory (*mufassira*) of *arsalna*, meaning: We said to them through the tongue of the Messenger, ﴿Worship Allah﴾.

The meaning of fa-buʿdan (فَبُعْداً) is: "they perished," as one says: baʿida baʿdan and buʿdan, like rashida rashadan and rushdan.

Lil-qawm al-ẓālimīn (لِلْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ) is an explanation of those against whom the curse of distance was invoked, like: hayta laka (هَيْتَ لَكَ), and li-mā tūʿadūn (ولِما تُوعَدُونَ).

Qurūnan (generations): the people of Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ, Shuʿayb, and others. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "Banū Isrāʾīl." Ajalahā (its term): the appointed time that was set for its destruction and recorded.

Tatran (تَتْرا): the alif is for the feminine (ta'nith), since "the messengers" (al-rusul) is a plural noun. It is also read tatran (تترى) with tanwin, and the taa' is a substitution for a waw, as in tawlaj (تولج) and tayqur (تيقور) [[His words "as in tawlaj and tayqur": al-tawlaj is the lair of wild beasts into which the animal enters. Sibawayh said: the taa' is substituted for a waw, and the form is fawʿal, as stated in al-Sihah. Also in it: tayqur, and waqar (dignity). Its origin is wayqur; the waw was changed into a taa'. End of quote. So its pattern is fayʿol. (ʿ)]], meaning: consecutive, one after another, from al-watr (الوتر), which is the single or odd one.

He attributed the messengers to Himself (exalted is He) and to their peoples, saying "Then We sent Our messengers" (ثُمَّ أَرْسَلْنا رُسُلَنا) and "their messengers came to them with the clear proofs" — because the idafa (annexation) is by way of association, and the messenger is connected to both the sender and the one sent to.

Wa lagad jaaathum rusuluna bil-bayyinat (وَلَقَدْ جاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُنا بِالْبَيِّناتِ) and (وَلَقَدْ جاءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُهُمْ بِالْبَيِّناتِ): "And indeed Our messengers came to them with the clear proofs," and "And indeed their messengers came to them with the clear proofs."

Fa-atba'na al-umam aw al-qurun ba'dahum ba'dan (فَأَتْبَعْنا الأمم أو القرون بَعْضَهُمْ بَعْضاً): "So We made the nations, or the generations, follow one another" in destruction (fi al-ihlak).

Wa ja'alnahum ahadith (وَجَعَلْناهُمْ أخبارا): "And We made them tales" to be talked about and marvelled at (يسمر بها ويتعجب منها).

Al-ahadith (الأحاديث): it may be the plural-collective (ism jam') of hadith (حديث), and from it: "the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It may also be the plural of uhdutha (أحدوثة), which is like udhuhka (الأضحوكة), al-alʿuba (الألعوبة) and al-aʿjuba (الأعجوبة). It is what people talk about for amusement and wonder, and this is what is meant here.

Q: What is meant by "clear authority" (al-sultan al-mubin)?

A: It is permissible that it means the staff, for it was the mother of Musa's signs and the first of them, and various miracles were connected to it: its turning into a serpent, its swallowing what the magicians had faked, the splitting of the sea, the gushing of springs from the rock when he struck it with it, its being a guard (for sheep), a candle (torch), a green fruit-bearing tree, and a bucket and rope. It has been treated as if it were not part of the others, because of the excellence it had over them; therefore it was joined to them by conjunction (ʿataftu), like the words of Allah the Exalted: "and Jibril and Mikail" (Qur'an 2:98).

It is also permissible that what is meant is the signs themselves, i.e., they are signs and a clear proof.

﴿To Firʿawn and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Firʿawn, and the command of Firʿawn was not rightly guided.﴾ (This follows the surrounding verses.)

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verse 50:**

If it is asked: "If it had been said as two signs, would that have had a rationale?" I answer: Yes, because Mary bore a child without being touched, and ʿĪsā was a spirit from God that He cast to her. He spoke in the cradle, he brought the dead to life, and there were other miracles. So he was a sign in more than one respect. The wording permits the dual on the assumption that the original was ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ آيَةً وَأُمَّهُ آيَةً﴾ ("And We made the son of Maryam a sign and his mother a sign"), and then the first ﴿آيَةً﴾ was omitted because the second indicates it.

*al-rabwa* and *al-rubāwa*: the vowels (*ḥarakāt*, the short vowel signs) on their letter *rāʾ* differ. It is also read *rabwa* and *rubāwa* with a *ḍamma* (the *u* vowel), and *rubāwa* with a *kasra* (the *i* vowel). It means a raised land. It was said: it is Iliya, the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and that it is the navel of the earth and the nearest part of the earth to the heavens by eighteen miles, from Kaʿb. It was also said: it is Damascus and its Ghouta.

From al-Ḥasan: Filastin (Palestine) and al-Ramla. From Abu Hurayrah: "Keep to this Ramla, the Ramla of Filastin, for it is the *rabwa* that Allah mentioned." It was also said: Egypt.

*al-qarār*: a settled place of level, flat ground. From Qatadah: "[It is] with fruits and water," meaning that its inhabitants settle there for the sake of the fruits.

*al-maʿīn*: the water that is visible and flows on the surface of the earth. Scholars differ on whether its *mīm* is an added letter or a original root letter. The reasoning of one who makes it a *mafʿūl* (the *maf‘ūl* pattern, a passive participle) is that it is perceived by the eye because it is visible, from *ʿānahu*, meaning "he perceived it with his eye," like *rakabahu*, meaning "he struck him with his knee." The reasoning of one who makes it a *faʿīl* (the *faʿīl* pattern, an intensive or active form) is that it is beneficial through its visibility and flow, from *al-māʿūn*, which means benefit.

This address and speech are not to be taken literally, for how could they be, since the messengers were sent at different times and in different eras? The meaning is only to inform that every messenger, in his own time, was addressed with this, ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, and was enjoined to it. The listener should then believe that a command which all the messengers were addressed with and enjoined to is worthy of being followed and acted upon.

[[Mahmud said: "This address and speech are not to be taken literally, for how could they be, since the messengers were sent at different times and in different eras. The meaning is only to inform that every messenger, in his own time, was addressed with this." Ahmad said: This is a Mu'tazili (Mu'tazilah, the rationalist school) whiff. The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) is that God, exalted is He, is eternally a speaker who commands and forbids, and the realization of a command does not require the presence of the addressee. On this basis, His words ﴿eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾ are to be taken literally and in their real sense according to the People of Truth. It is eternally established, whether the addressees exist at a given time, dispersed as in this address, or gathered as he claims. The Mu'tazila, because they rejected belief in the eternity of speech, slipped, so that they interpreted this verse and its like as metaphor and contrary to the apparent meaning. What is wrong with al-Zamakhshari, singling out this verse as contrary to the apparent meaning, when his creed requires taking similar words of God, such as ﴿establish prayer and give zakat﴾, and all general commands to the community, as contrary to the apparent meaning?]] and it was enjoined upon them. The intended meaning of "the good things" (al-tayyibat) is what is lawful and good.

It was said: the good provision is lawful, pure and sustaining. The lawful is that in which God is not disobeyed; the pure is that in which God is not forgotten; and the sustaining is that which keeps the soul and preserves the intellect.

Or what is meant is what is pleasing and delicious of foods and fruits. This is supported by its coming directly after His words ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of settlement and flowing water﴾. It is also possible that this informing took place at the time when Jesus and Mary were given refuge on the high ground. It is then mentioned by way of narration, meaning: We gave them refuge and said to them this, that is, We informed them that all the messengers were addressed with this. So: ﴿So eat of what We have provided, and do righteous deeds﴾, following the messengers.

The passage is read as follows: "wa-inna" with a kasra, on the basis of resumption (*isti'nâf*, beginning a new sentence). "Wa-anna" is taken to mean "wa-li-anna" ("and because"), and "anna" is the lightened form (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*, the light form of the heavy *inna*), with "ummatukum" in the nominative after it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verse 53:

It is also read *zuburan*, the plural of *zabur* (a book), meaning: books of different kinds, that is, they made their religion into many religions. *Zuburan* (in the sense of) pieces: it is borrowed from *zabr* (bars or ingots) of silver and iron. *Zubaran*, with the *ba'* lightened, is like *rusul* with *rusl*: that is, every sect of these people who differ and have split their religion into parts rejoices in its falsehood, is content in mind, and believes that it is upon the truth.

Ghamra: the water that covers a person's height. He used it as a metaphor for what they are immersed in of ignorance and blindness. Or they were likened to players in a flood of water, because of the falsehood they were engaged in. He said:

ليالي اللهو يطبينى فأتبعه ... كأننى ضارب في غمرة لعب

(Nights of pleasure call me, and I follow them, as if I were a swimmer in a flood of play.)

This is by Dhu al-Rummah. *Layali* is in the accusative as a *zarf* (adverb of time, a temporal complement), and *al-lahu* is the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence). *Yatbawuhu, yatbuhu* and *yatibuhu* mean: he called him and pulled him. *Tibi al-naqah thadyaha* means the she-camel's udder was pulled for milking. The meaning is: pleasure calls me on many nights, so I follow it, as if I were swimming in a sea of water that covers the height of a man, playing in it. *La'ib* is the second *khabar* (predicate). It is also narrated as *laghib*, with the dotted *ghayn*, from *al-lughub*, which means hardship. It is also said that *layali* is in the genitive construction with the clause after it, so it is a *zarf* for what precedes it. It is narrated as *al-lahi* in the genitive. And *tatbinī* is with a *ta'*, so the subject is the pronoun referring to *al-layali*.

It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding *fi ghamratihim hatta hin*: "until they are killed or die."

The Prophet ﷺ was consoled by this, and was forbidden to hasten their punishment or to be impatient about its delay. It is also read: ﴿يُمِدُّهُمْ﴾ (We extend to them), and ﴿يُسَارِعُ﴾ and ﴿يُسْرِعُ﴾ with the ya' (yuṣāri‘u, yusri‘u), the subject being Allah, glorified and exalted. It is permissible for [the verb] ﴿يُسَارِعُ﴾ and ﴿يُسْرِعُ﴾ to include a pronoun referring to what is extended ("that by which" they are extended). [It is also read] ﴿يُسَارَعُ﴾ in the passive. The meaning is: this extension is nothing but a gradual drawing-on (istidraj) of them toward sins and a dragging of them toward increased sin, while they think it is a hastening for them into good things and into what has benefit and honour for them, and an advance of reward before its time. It is also permissible that it refers to the recompense of good deeds, as is done with the people of goodness among the Muslims. And ﴿بَلْ﴾ (bal, "rather") is a corrective (istidrak) to His saying ﴿أَيَحْسَبُونَ﴾ (do they reckon...?), meaning:

Rather, they are like cattle, having neither discernment nor awareness, so that they would reflect and consider whether this is a drawing-on or a hastening into good. If you say: where is the returning pronoun from the predicate of inna to its subject, when its pronoun is not hidden in it?

I say: it is omitted, its estimated form being: "We hasten by it," "he hastens by it," "Allah hastens by it," like His saying ﴿إِنَّ ذَلِكَ لَمِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾ (indeed that is among the matters requiring resolve), i.e., "indeed that is from Him." This is because the speech is lengthy and there is no risk of confusion.

الَّذِينَ ﴿يُؤْتُونَ ما آتَوْا﴾ يعطون ما أعطوا. وفي قراءة رسول الله (ﷺ) وعائشة: ﴿يَأْتُونَ ما أَتَوْا﴾، أي يفعلون ما فعلوا. وعنها (رضي الله عنها) أنها قالت: قلت: يا رسول الله، هو الذي يزني ويسرق ويشرب الخمر وهو على ذلك يخاف الله؟ قال: "لا يا ابنة الصدّيق، ولكن هو الذي يصلي ويصوم ويتصدّق، وهو على ذلك يخاف الله أن لا يُقبل منه" [[أخرجه الترمذي، وابن ماجه، وأحمد، وإسحاق، وابن أبي شيبة، والحاكم، والبيهقي في الشُّعب، من رواية عبد الرحمن بن سعيد بن وهب الهمذاني عن عائشة قالت: سألت فذكره. قال الترمذي: وقد روي عن عبد الرحمن بن سعيد عن أبي حازم عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه. اهـ. وهذا الطريق أخرجه الطبري بهذا الإسناد أن عائشة قالت: فذكره، وله عنده طريق أخرى عن عائشة فيها ليث بن أبي سليم، وهو ضعيف. وقوله: وهو في قراءة النبي (ﷺ) وعائشة ﴿يُؤْتُونَ ما آتَوْا﴾: كأنه يشير إلى هذا الحديث. وأخرج منه ما أخرجه الحاكم من طريق عبد الله بن عمير عن أبيه أنه سأل عائشة عن قوله تعالى ﴿الَّذِينَ يُؤْتُونَ ما آتَوْا﴾: كيف كان (ﷺ) يقرؤها: يُؤْتون: يَأْتون أو يُؤْتون؟ قالت: أيهما أحب إليك؟ قال: الذين يأتون ما أتوا. قالت: أشهد أن رسول الله (ﷺ) كان يقرؤها، وكذلك أُنزلت. وفي إسناده يحيى بن راشد وهو ضعيف. وله طريق أخرى عند أحمد من طريق أبي خلف الجمحي: أن عبيد بن عمير سأل عائشة نحوه، وفيه إسماعيل بن مسلم المكي، وهو ضعيف.]] ﴿يُسارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْراتِ﴾ يحتمل معنيين: أحدهما: أن يراد يرغبون في الطاعات أشد الرغبة فيبادرونها. والثاني: أنهم يتعجلون في الدنيا المنافع ووجوه الإكرام، كما قال تعالى: ﴿فَآتاهُمُ اللَّهُ ثَوابَ الدُّنْيا وَحُسْنَ ثَوابِ الْآخِرَةِ﴾، و﴿وَآتَيْناهُ أَجْرَهُ فِي الدُّنْيا وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾، لأنهم إذا سُوِّرع بها لهم فقد سارعوا في نيلها وتعجّلوها. وهذا الوجه أحسن طباقًا للآية المتقدمة، لأن فيه إثبات ما نفي عن الكفار للمؤمنين. وقُرئ: ﴿يُسْرِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْراتِ﴾. ﴿لَها سابِقُونَ﴾ أي فاعلون السبق لأجلها، أو سابقون الناس لأجلها، أو إياها سابقون، أي: ينالونها قبل الآخرة حيث عُجّلت لهم في الدنيا. ويجوز أن يكون ﴿لَها سابِقُونَ﴾ خبرًا بعد خبر. ومعنى ﴿وَهُمْ لَها﴾ كمعنى قوله:

أنتَ لها أحمدُ من بين البشرْ [[قصيدة رائقة صُغتها ... أنتَ لها أحمدُ من بين البشرْ

رائقة: مُحالية من الحشو والتعقيد. وصُغتها، بالتشديد، للمبالغة. وأنت لها: أي أهلٌ وكفؤ لها. وأحمد: منادى.

ومن بين البشر: متعلق بمحذوف حال، أي: منتخبًا من بينهم. ويجوز أن يكون أحمد أفعل تفضيل، كذا قيل.

للأعشى الحرمازي. وضمير ﴿لها﴾ مبهم يفسره قوله: «داهية الدهر»، أي: الشديدة المهمة من شدائده. والصمّاء: الصلبة. والغبر، كسبب، بمعنى البقية، من غبر إذا بقي، أو من الغبار، أو من الظلمة. وأصل «صمّاء الغبر»: الحية تسكن في منقع قرب مويهة فلا تُقرب، ويُضرب بها المثل. والمعنى: أنها تغشى فلا يُهتدى إلى التخلص منها. ومنذرٌ: منادى، وروي بدله: أحمدُ. وقيل: ضمير ﴿لها﴾ للنبوة.]]

أنتَ لها أحمدُ من بين البشرْ [[قصيدة رائقة صُغتها ... أنتَ لها أحمدُ من بين البشرْ

رائقة: مُحالية من الحشو والتعقيد. وصُغتها، بالتشديد، للمبالغة. وأنت لها: أي أهلٌ وكفؤ لها. وأحمد: منادى.

أنتَ لها أحمدُ من بين البشرْ [[قصيدة رائقة صُغتها ... أنتَ لها أحمدُ من بين البشرْ

رائقة: مُحالية من الحشو والتعقيد. وصُغتها، بالتشديد، للمبالغة. وأنت لها: أي أهلٌ وكفؤ لها. وأحمد: منادى.

ومن بين البشر: متعلق بمحذوف حال، أي: منتخبًا من بينهم. ويجوز أن يكون أحمد أفعل تفضيل، كذا قيل.

Its meaning: that which He has described the righteous as having is not beyond the limit of their capacity and ability. Likewise, everything He has obligated His servants with, and the deeds they have performed, are not lost before Him; rather, they are recorded with Him in a Book, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh) or the record of deeds, which speaks with the truth. On the Day of Resurrection they will read from it only what is true and just, with no addition or deficiency, and not one of them will be wronged. Or it may be that He intends: God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (wus'), so if the obligated person does not reach being in the state of these foremost ones, after exerting his utmost effort and expending his ability, then he bears no blame; and with Us is a Book in which the deeds of the foremost and the moderate are recorded, and We do not wrong anyone of his due, nor lower him below his rank. Rather, the hearts of the disbelievers are in a deep heedlessness of this, that is, of what these described believers are upon. And they have deeds beyond that, exceeding and surpassing it, meaning: compared to what the believers were described with, they are accustomed to those deeds and addicted to them, and they are not weaned from them until God seizes them with punishment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verses 64–67:

"Hatta" (until) here is the particle after which speech begins. The speech is the conditional sentence. The punishment (al-'adhab) is their being killed on the day of Badr. Or it is hunger, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them and said: "O Allah, press down Your foot upon Mudar, and make it for them years like the years of Yusuf." [Agreed upon, from a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and it will come in full in the tafsir of Surah al-Dukhan.] So Allah afflicted them with famine until they ate carrion, dogs, burnt bones, "al-qadd" [Note: his saying "al-qadd" in al-Sihah is "al-qadd," with a kasra: a strip cut from untanned hide. (A)] and their children.

Al-ju'ar: the outcry of one calling for help. He said: "A crier at the hours of sleep to his Lord."

That is, it will be said to them then: ﴿Do not cry out today﴾, for the outcry will not benefit you. ﴿From Us you will not be helped﴾: you will not be aided or protected from Us, or on Our part; no help or rescue will reach you.

They said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Ancient House (al-bayt al-'atiq) or to the Sacred Precinct (al-haram). They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Haram." What permitted this implied reference is their well-known pride in the House, and that they had no glory except that they were its custodians and those who tended it. It is also permissible that it refers to "My verses," but it is in the masculine because it carries the meaning of "My Book." The meaning of their arrogance toward the Qur'an is their denying it out of arrogance.

"Mustakbirin" is taken to imply "mukadhdhibin" (those who deny), so it takes the same construction. Or: their hearing of it causes arrogance and insolence in you, so you are arrogant because of it. Or the "ba'" (with) is connected to "sāmiran" (talking together at night), meaning: you keep up talk about the Qur'an and slander it. They used to gather around the House at night, conversing by night (yasmarun), and most of their night talk was about the Qur'an, calling it magic and poetry, and cursing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Or: "tahjurun" (you speak abusively). The "sāmir" is like "hādir" in its general use for a group. It is also read "sumaran" and "sammaran." "Tahjurun" and "tahjurun" are from "ahjara" in his speech when he used foul language. "Al-hujr" with a damma is obscenity, and from "hajara," which is intensive, when one rambles in delirium. "Al-hajr" with a fatha is delirium.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not revile Mudar, nor Rabi'a, for they were both Muslims. Do not revile Qass, for he was a Muslim. Do not revile al-Harith ibn Ka'b, nor Asad ibn Khuzayma, nor Tamim ibn Murr, for they were upon Islam. And whatever doubt you have about it [i.e. about anything of this], do not doubt that Tubba' was a Muslim." [Note: the exegete Mukhrij limited the attribution of the first sentence to al-Suhayli from al-Zubayr, and it includes the rest. It was also transmitted by Ibn Sa'd and al-Baladhuri through the route of Sa'd ibn Abi Ayyub from 'Abd Allah ibn Khalid, that he was informed that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile Mudar, for he was a Muslim." As for Tubba', al-Fakihi narrated through the route of 'Umar ibn Jabir from Sahl ibn Sa'd, raised to the Prophet: "Do not revile Tubba', for he has embraced Islam." al-Hakim transmitted it through the route of Ibn Jurayj from al-Zuhri from 'Urwa from 'A'isha, who said: "Tubba' was a righteous man..." the hadith, [which is] mawquf (halted at a companion). And his saying: "And the sermon that Abu Talib gave at the marriage of Khadija bint Khuwaylid, may God be pleased with her, suffices, with its crying out, as a herald." I say: the text also supports this.]

And it is narrated that Dabba was a Muslim, and that he was in charge of the police of Sulayman ibn Dawud.

[They did not] recognise Muhammad and the soundness of his lineage, his residing in the midst of the Hashim clan, his trustworthiness, his truthfulness, his nobility, his intellect, and his being characterised as the best of the youths of Quraysh; and the sermon that Abu Talib gave at the marriage of Khadija bint Khuwaylid suffices, with its crying out.

[Their accusation was] madness (al-janna). They knew that he was innocent of it and that he was the most sound of them in intellect and the most penetrating in mind. But he brought them what opposed their desires and whims, and did not agree with what they had been raised upon, and [the truth] was mixed into their flesh and blood against following falsehood. They could find no rejection of it nor any way to repel it, because it is the clear truth and the straight path. So they inclined to bewilderment and relied upon lying, by attributing to him madness, sorcery and poetry.

[Note: "wa-sayyata bi-luhumihim" means: mixed.]

If you say: His saying "and most of them" implies that few of them did not dislike the truth. I say: among them was one who abandoned faith in it out of pride and disdain, from fear of being rebuked by his people, and that they would say "he has turned away" and abandoned the religion of his fathers, not from dislike of the truth, as is related about Abu Talib.

[Note: Mahmud [al-Zamakhshari] said: "If you say: 'most of them' implies that few of them do not dislike the truth, and how is that, when all of them are disbelievers? I say: among them were those who refused Islam out of caution against opposing their fathers and against being said to have 'turned away,' like Abu Talib, not from dislike of the truth." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: Better than this is that the pronoun in His saying "and most of them" refers to the genus of people as a whole. When He mentioned this group from the genus, the statement "and most of them" remained referring to the genus in its totality, like His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers﴾ [26:8], and His saying: ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should strive, will not be believers﴾ [12:103]. This is shown by His saying: ﴿But He has brought them the truth﴾ [23:70], and the Prophet (ﷺ) came to all people and was sent to the whole of humanity. It is possible also to take "most" as "all," just as "few" is taken as negation. And God knows best. As for the statement of al-Zamakhshari that one who persists in disbelief and prefers to remain upon it by imitating his fathers "is not averse to the truth," this is rejected, for whoever loves a thing dislikes its opposite. So when they love to remain in disbelief, they necessarily dislike transferring from it to faith, and God knows best. Then the discussion moved to the improbability of Abu Talib's faith. The verification of the matter is that he died upon disbelief, and the reason for this is that he was the most famous of the Prophet's paternal uncles. If he had embraced Islam, his Islam would have become famous, as the Islam of al-'Abbas and Hamza became famous, and more fittingly, because he was more famous. The one who holds that he became a Muslim may excuse the absence of his fame by saying he only embraced Islam shortly before death, so no stances in Islam were manifested by him by which he would be known, as they were manifested by the other uncles of the Prophet (peace be upon him). This, and the apparent [meaning] is that he did not embrace Islam. Sufficient as proof of this is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "I asked God concerning him," and that he is after that in a shallow fire, whose head boils from his feet. If it is said: this does not necessitate his death upon disbelief, because many sinful monotheists are punished with more than that. We say: whoever affirms his Islam claims that this was shortly before death, and Islam wipes away what came before it, and that moment in which he became one of the Muslims does not bear the sins that would require that. And God knows best.]

If you say: some people claim that Abu Talib's Islam was sound. I say: Glory be to God! As if Abu Talib was the most obscure of the uncles of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), so that the Islam of Hamza and al-'Abbas, may God be pleased with them, would become famous while the Islam of Abu Talib would remain hidden!

For this reason the reading of the one who read kharjan fa-kharāj rabbika is good, meaning: "Or do you ask them for a payment for your guidance to them? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verse 78–80:

It is only that He singled out the hearing, the sight and the hearts, because there are attached to them benefits, religious and worldly, that are not attached to anything else. The foremost of their benefits is that they should employ their hearing and their sight upon the signs and acts of God, and then reflect and draw inference with their hearts. Whoever does not employ them for what they were created for is in the position of one who lacks them, as God the Exalted said: ﴿So their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight, nor their hearts, in anything, since they used to deny the signs of God﴾. The foremost of the thanks for the blessing in them is acknowledging the Bestower of it, and that one does not make for Him any equal or partner. That is: "You give very little thanks." Here "mā" is an intensifying addition, meaning "truly." ﴿He it is Who created you (dhara'akum) and multiplied you through procreation; and to Him you will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day﴾, that is: He alone is specific to it, and He is the one who governs it, and none other is able to direct them. It is also recited "ya'qilūn" (they reason) with the letter ya', from Abu 'Amr.

That is: the people of Makkah said what the disbelievers before them had said. *Al-asatir* (the myths, or legends): the plural of *asțar*, which is itself the plural of *saṭr* (a line).

Ru'bah said:

*Verily I, and the lines that were inscribed, inscribed in writing,*
*For one who says: "O Nasr, Nasr, Nasr!"*

[[Verily I, and the lines that were inscribed, inscribed in writing... for one who says: "O Nasr, Nasr, Nasr!"

By Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj. The meaning of *al-asṭār* here is writing. It is the plural of *saṭr*, with a vowel on the first letter, and its origin is a verbal noun, like *al-sākin* (the stationary) and *al-wast* (the middle).

*Suṭirn* is in the passive voice (*mabni lil-majhul*). *Saṭran* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). *Li-qā'il* is the predicate (*khabar*) of *inni*, and what lies between them is a parenthetical oath clause (*jumla qasamiyya i'tiraḍiyya*). *Naṣr* is indeclinable, built on a *ḍamma* (*mabni 'ala al-ḍamm*), and he is Ibn Sayyar, the king of Khurasan. The second *Naṣr* is a verbal emphasis (*tawkid lafzi*) and is in the nominative according to its form. The third is likewise, but in the accusative according to its position, because it is a definite single word that is a follower. Or it is a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, meaning: "Help me with help." It has been said that the second is *Naḍr* with a dotted *ḍ*, as a proper name for the companion of the first *Naṣr*, and then the conjunction is omitted. From Abu 'Ubaydah: what is transmitted is that the one with the dotted *ḍ* is the third, who was the chamberlain of Naṣr, and the poet complained about him to Naṣr, so Naṣr made him accusative as an incitement (*al-ighra'*). The meaning according to the first reading:

*"By the right of the inscribed Book, I am seeking help from him, and from no one else."*]]

These are what the earlier people wrote, which have no reality. The plural *asāṭīr* is more fitting for *ustūra* (a myth).

﴿Will you not fear Him?﴾ That is, will you not fear Him, so that you do not associate partners with Him and disobey His messengers.

"Ajarta fulanan ala fulan" means: when you rescue someone from another and protect him from him. The meaning is: He rescues whom He wills from whom He wills, and no one can rescue anyone from Him.

﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ That is, you are deceived away from His oneness and obedience. The deceiver is Satan and desire.

Recited also: "atayhum" and "ataytuhum" (with fatha and with damma). "bi-l-haqq" (with truth): that attributing a son to Him is impossible, and association (shirk) is false. "wa-innahum la-kadhibun" (and indeed they are liars), in that they claim for Him a son while also making a partner with Him.

﴿Since there is not with Him any god; otherwise each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others.﴾ That is, were there many gods, each one would have singled out what he created and claimed it for himself exclusively. You would then have seen the kingdom of each one of them distinct from the kingdoms of the others, and some of them would have prevailed over others, just as you see the situation of the kings of the world: their realms are separate and they contend with one another. Since you have not seen any sign of separate kingdoms or of mutual contention, know that He is one God, in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of everything.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verses 93–95:

Ma and the nun (ma wa-l-nun): both are emphatic (muakkidatan), meaning: if it is necessary that You show me what You promise them of punishment, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, then do not make me a companion to them (fa-la taj'alni qarinan lahum), and do not punish me with their punishment.

From al-Hasan: Allah informed him (the Prophet) that there would be a vengeance (niqmah) against his community, but did not inform him whether it would be during his lifetime or after his death. So He commanded him to make this supplication.

If you say: how is it permissible for Allah to make His prophet, who is protected from sin (al-ma'sum), to be with the wrongdoers, so that he would ask not to be made among them? I say: it is permissible for a servant to ask his Lord for what he knows he will not do, and to seek refuge in Him from what he knows he will not do, in order to manifest servanthood (ubudiyyah), humility before his Lord, and submission to Him (ikhbat). And the Prophet's seeking forgiveness (istighfar) when he rose from his assembly, seventy times or a hundred times, was for this reason. How excellent is al-Hasan's saying about the words of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, "I have been put in charge of you, though I am not the best of you": he knew that he was the best of them, but the believer diminishes himself (yahdim nafsahu).

It was read: inma tur'innahum, with a hamza, instead of turini (in place of turini)[[The note reads: "the reading 'inma tur'innahum with the hamza' — in another copy: 'inma turi'ni with the hamza, as it was read...' (a)]], as in the reading: fa-imma tar'an, wa-latar'awunna al-jahim. And it is weak.

His saying "My Lord" twice, before the condition and before the response, encourages the excellence of humble supplication and loud entreaty (wa-ju'ar). They used to deny the promise of punishment and mock it, and their hastening of it was for that reason. So it was said to them: Allah is able to fulfil what He has promised, if you reflect. So what is the basis of this denial?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on surah 23, verse 96:

It is more eloquent than saying "repel the bad deed with the good deed" (*bi-l-hasanah al-sayyi'ah*), because of the superlative it contains, as if he had said: "Repel with the best (*al-husna*) the bad deed."

The meaning is: pardon their offence and meet it with the greatest possible kindness, so that when pardon and kindness are combined and one exerts one's utmost effort in them, the good deed becomes doubled against a single bad deed. This is the implication of His words ﴿with that which is better﴾ [[Mahmud said: "This is more eloquent than saying: repel the bad deed with the good deed, because of the superlative it contains, as if he had said: repel with the best (*al-husna*) the bad deed. The meaning is: pardon their offence and meet it with the greatest possible kindness, so that when pardon and kindness are combined and one exerts one's utmost effort in them, the good deed becomes doubled against a single bad deed. This is the implication of His words: ﴿with that which is better﴾." Ahmad said: What he has mentioned as establishing a comparison (*mufadalah*) is an expression of sharing in a matter and distinction from others, and there is no sharing between the good deed and the bad deed, for they are opposites (*didan*) that stand in contrast. How then can comparison be realized? I say: The intended meaning is that the good deed, as a member of the category of good deeds, exceeds the bad deed as a member of the category of bad deeds, so the comparison falls under something more general than whether this is a good deed and that is a bad deed. This is the case with every comparison between two opposites, like the saying: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," meaning that among sweet things it is distinguished from vinegar among sour things, not that there is a special sharing between them.]].

From this category is what is related of Ash'ab the jester, that he said: "Al-A'mash and I were raised in the lap of so-and-so. He kept raising and lowering us until we became equal," meaning that both of them reached the utmost limit in what each of them attained: Ash'ab reached the utmost limit in lowliness, and al-A'mash reached the utmost limit in nobility. This is the explanation of his words about himself. Let us return to the verse and say: it admits another, closer form of comparison:

It is that the comparison is between the good deeds by which the bad deed is repelled. For it may be repelled by pardon and forbearance, and one may be content with repelling it by that alone. Yet honour may be added to pardon, and its utmost limit is reached by exerting one's full effort. All these kinds of repelling are repelling by a good deed, but the best of these good deeds for repelling is the last, because it includes a number of good deeds. Thus the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to use the best of good deeds in repelling the bad deed. On this reading the comparison is taken in its true sense without any need for interpretation, and God knows best.

Consider this, for it is very good.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that it is the testimony that there is no god but God, and the bad deed is polytheism (*shirk*).

It is related from Mujahid: "The greeting (*al-salam*): he greets him when he meets him." And from al-Hasan: "Forbearance and pardon." It has also been said that it is abrogated (*mansukh*) by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*, the verse commanding fighting), and it has been said that it is muhkam (*muhkamah*, not abrogated), because conciliation is encouraged so long as it does not lead to the corruption of religion or the disparagement of honour. ﴿What they describe﴾: what they mention of your circumstances, contrary to your real condition, or their description of you and their evil speech. ﴿And God knows that better than you and is more capable of requiting them﴾, and God knows best.

Al-Hamz: prodding. Al-hamazat (the "pricks" or "promptings") is the plural of the single instance of it. From it comes mihmaz (the goad) of the horse-trainer. The meaning is that the devils urge people toward sins and incite them to them, just as a horse-breaker prods the beasts to make them walk. Akin to hamz is al-azz in the words of the Exalted, ﴿tu'uzzuhum azza﴾ (﴿they incite them with incitement﴾). It is a command to seek refuge from their pricks in the manner of one who supplicates to his Lord, repeating his call, and to seek refuge from their coming near him at all and hovering around him. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both:

"At the recitation of the Qur'an." And from 'Ikrimah: "At the time of death (al-naza')."

*So if you wish, I shall forbid women other than you.*[[The explanation of this line was given earlier, in volume two, page 383; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

And His saying:

*Ala, have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad,*
*For if I am not worthy, You are worthy of it.*

Here "Ala" is an opening particle indicating attention to what follows, and he addressed the One, the Unique God, with the plural form, following the Arab custom of addressing lords and kings in this way out of exaltation. It is said that the repetition is an indication of repeating the verb for emphasis, as if it were said: "Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, have mercy on me." Its attribution to Muhammad (ﷺ) is for seeking a means of approach to God, Mighty and Majestic, for if I am not worthy of this request, or of the mercy and gentleness that is requested, then You, O God, are worthy of it.

When one becomes certain of death and perceives the reality of the matter, regret overtakes him for what he neglected of faith and righteous deeds. So he asks his Lord for a return, and says: ﴿لَعَلِّي أَعْمَلُ صَالِحًا فِيمَا تَرَكْتُ﴾ (*that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind*), in the faith that he abandoned. The meaning is: "Perhaps I may bring about what I left of faith and do righteous deeds in it, just as you say: 'Perhaps I may build upon a foundation,' meaning: 'I establish a foundation and build upon it.'" It is also said: "in what I left of wealth."

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the believer sees the angels, they say: 'We will return you to the world.' He says: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows! Rather, (I go) forward to God.' As for the disbeliever, he says: 'My Lord, return me!'"

﴿كَلَّا﴾ (*No!*) is a rebuke against seeking a return, and a denial and a deeming it remote.

By "the word" (al-kalima) is meant the group of speech that is ordered with some of its parts linked to others, and it is His saying: ﴿لَعَلِّي أَعْمَلُ صَالِحًا فِيمَا تَرَكْتُ﴾. Or it means: "He alone is its speaker, and he is not answered in it, nor is it heard from him." ﴿وَمِنْ وَرَائِهِمْ بَرْزَخٌ﴾ (*and behind them is a barrier*): the pronoun refers to the group. That is, in front of them there is a barrier between them and return until the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is not that they will return on the Day of Resurrection; rather, it is a total despair, since it is known that there is no return on the Day of Resurrection except to the Hereafter.

The Horn (al-Sur) is read with an open waw (aṣ-ṣawr), according to al-Hasan. It is read as aṣ-ṣūr (with a kasra or fatha), according to Abu Razin. This is evidence for the one who interprets aṣ-ṣūr as the plural of ṣūrah (form), and who negates kinship. It is possible that severance will occur among them when they scatter, some to punishment and some to reward. Ties and affection among them will exist only through deeds, so kinship is nullified and invalidated. Kinship is not counted on the Day, because compassion and mercy between relatives will have vanished, as a person flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he read ﴿وَلا يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ with the ta' assimilated into the sin.

If you say: this contradicts the statement ﴿وَلا يَسْئَلُ حَمِيمٌ حَمِيماً﴾ (and no intimate friend will ask about an intimate friend), and His statement ﴿وَأَقْبَلَ بَعْضُهُمْ عَلى بَعْضٍ يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾ (and some of them will turn to others, questioning one another). [Mahmud said: "If you say this contradicts His statement, 'Some of them will turn to others, questioning one another.'" Ahmad said: One should not take this course in raising objections concerning the benefits of the Mighty Book, which falsehood cannot approach from before it or behind it, a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy. The proper way of asking is to say: "My understanding falls short of reconciling these two verses; what is their correct interpretation?" Had a questioner asked ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) about something from the Book of Allah in this form, he would have struck his back with the ad-durra (whip).] And His statement ﴿يَتَعارَفُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ (they will recognize one another). How is harmonization between them achieved? I say: there are two answers to this. The first: the Day of Resurrection's duration is fifty thousand years, and it contains different times and conditions; they question and recognize one another in some of them, and in others they do not perceive that because of the severity of terror and dread. [His speech returned to answering the question. He said: "The way to reconcile them is to understand that as differing according to the stations of the Resurrection." Ahmad said: Az-Zamakhshari often seizes the opportunity to deny intercession, and gathers his skirts to refute those who affirm it, whenever he reaches a statement such as ﴿وَلا تَنْفَعُها شَفاعَةٌ﴾ (and no intercession will benefit it), and ﴿لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ وَلا خُلَّةٌ وَلا شَفاعَةٌ﴾ (no trade, no friendship, and no intercession). He then ignores the way of reconciling what apparently negates intercession with what apparently affirms it, by taking the matter as differing conditions on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah is the Granter of success.] The second: the mutual non-recognition occurs at the first blast of the Horn; when the second blast comes, they rise, recognize one another, and question one another.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verse 102–104:

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "al-Mawazin" (the scales) is the plural of "mawzun" (weighed), and it refers to the weighed deeds, namely the righteous deeds that have weight and value with God, from the words of the Exalted: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Therein they will abide forever.﴾

It is a substitute (badal) for "they have lost their souls," and there is no place in grammatical terms (mahall) for the substitute and the substituted, because the relative clause (silah) has no place in grammatical terms. Or it is a predicate after a predicate for "ulaʾika" (those).

Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿taLfahu﴾ means ﴿tasfaʿu﴾ (scorches). Al-Zajjaj said: "al-lafh" and "al-nafh" are the same, except that "al-lafh" has a stronger effect. And "al-kulooh" is when the two lips contract and draw back from the teeth, as you see roasted heads. On the authority of Malik ibn Dinar: the cause of the repentance of ʿUtba the boy was that he passed by a head taken out of the oven in the marketplace, and he fainted for three days and their nights.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Fire will roast it, so its upper lip will contract until it reaches the middle of his head, and its lower lip will hang down until it reaches his navel." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab, from the narration of Abu al-Samah from al-Haytham ibn Abi Saʿid.]]

And it has been read as "kalihoon" (kalihun).
