The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 23, verses 105–108:

Ghalabat ʿalaynā shiqwatunā: "Our wretchedness overcame us" (ghalabat ʿalaynā) means "our possession (milkatunā) overcame us," from your saying, "So-and-so overcame me in such-and-such," when he took it from you and possessed it. Al-shaqāwah (wretchedness) is the evil outcome that God knew they deserved because of their evil deeds. It is read shiqwatunā and shaqāwatunā, with the shīn both fatḥah and kasrah in both forms. ﴿Be silent therein﴾ (ikhsaʾū fīhā) means: be humiliated therein and be repelled, as dogs are repelled when they are driven away. It is said: khasaʾa al-kalb and khasaʾa bi-nafsihi (the dog was driven off, and it withdrew of itself). [[The saying "It is said: khasaʾa al-kalb… etc." In al-Sihah: khasaʾtu al-kalb and khasaʾa bi-nafsihi: it is transitive and intransitive. (ʿ)]]

﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ (wa-lā tukallimūn) concerning the lifting of the punishment, for it will not be lifted or lightened. It is said that this is the last speech they utter; after that there is no speech, only sighing, groaning and howling like the howling of dogs, without understanding and without being understood.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that they have six supplications. When they enter the Fire, they say ﴿Our Lord, You have made us see and hear﴾ for a thousand years, and they are answered: ﴿The word from Me has come true﴾. Then they call out for a thousand years: ﴿Our Lord, You have made us die twice﴾, and they are answered: ﴿That is because when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved﴾. Then they call out for a thousand years: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us﴾, and they are answered: ﴿You shall remain﴾.

Then they call out for a thousand years: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾, and they are answered: ﴿Did you not used to swear﴾. Then they call out for a thousand years: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out, and we will do righteous deeds﴾, and they are answered: ﴿Did We not give you long life?﴾. Then they call out for a thousand years: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾, and they are answered: ﴿Be silent therein﴾.

In Ubayy's reading, it is "أنه كان فريق" with a fatha on the hamza, in the sense of "لأنه" (because).

Al-sukhriyy, with a damma or a kasra, is a verbal noun of sakhara, like al-sukhr. However, the nisba ya' adds an intensification to the verb, just as it is said al-khususiyyah (particularity) from al-khusus. It is reported from al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' that the kasra form means mockery (al-huzu'), while the damma form means subjugation and servitude (al-sukhrah wa al-ubudiyyah), i.e., "tasakhkharuhum" and "ista'badtumuhum" (you made them serve you). The first view is the position of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. It has been said they are the Companions; it has also been said they are specifically the people of the Suffah. Its meaning: you took them as objects of mockery and busied yourselves with them scoffing, "until they made you forget My remembrance" (حَتَّى أَنْسَوْكُمْ ذِكْرِي), by your preoccupation with them in that state, so you abandoned it, i.e., you abandoned remembering Me and thus fearing Me regarding My friends.

It is also read as "أَنَّهُمْ" with a fatha. The kasra reading is then a fresh sentence, meaning: they have indeed triumphed because they were patient, so they were rewarded for their patience with the best reward. With the fatha, it is the object of "jazaytuhum" (I rewarded them), as in your saying: "jazaytuhum fawzahum" (I rewarded them their triumph).

Commentary: The reading "qāla" is in the codices of the people of Kufa. "Qul" is in the codices of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), Basra and Syria. In "qāla" the pronoun refers to God, or to the one commanded to question them from among the angels; in "qul" the pronoun refers to the Angel (Malik), or to some of the chiefs of the people of the Fire.

They made little of the length of their stay in the world, in comparison with their eternal abiding and with what they are suffering in it, because the one being tested feels the days of his trial to be long, and considers the days of ease that passed before it to be short. Or because they were in pleasure, and days of pleasure are short. Or because what has passed is as though it had never been. God confirmed them in their saying concerning the number of years they stayed in the world, and rebuked them for the heedlessness in which they were.

It has also been read, "fa-sal al-ʿādīn" (ask those who count). The meaning: we do not know the number of those years except that we consider them few, and reckon them a day or part of a day, because of what we are in of punishment, and we are not in a state to count them. So ask the one among them who is able to count, and the one who can direct his thought to it. It was said: ask the angels who count the lifespans of the servants and record their deeds.

It has also been read "al-ʿādδīn" with lightening of the consonant (i.e., al-ʿādīn), meaning: the wrongdoers, for they say what we say. And it has been read "al-ʿādiyīn", meaning: the ancient long-lived ones, for they make such lifespans seem short, so how about those who came after them?

From Ibn ʿAbbas: "He made them forget what they were in of punishment between the two blasts."

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 23, verses 115–118:**

*ʿAbathan* is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a grammatical term for an accusative that describes the state of the subject at the time of the action), meaning: *ʿābithīn*, "playing about," like His saying ﴿*lāʿibīn*﴾ ("playing"). Or it is an accusative of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*, an accusative giving the reason for the action), meaning: We did not create you for play. Nothing moved Us to create you except a wisdom that required it, namely that We should worship you and impose on you the hardships of obedience and the abandonment of sins, and then return you from the abode of obligation to the abode of recompense, so that We reward the good-doer and punish the wrongdoer. ﴿*wa-annakum ilaynā lā turjaʿūn*﴾ ("and that you would not be returned to Us") is coordinated with ﴿*annamā khalaqnākum*﴾ ("that We created you"). It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with *ʿabathan*, meaning: "for play, and for your being left without being returned."

It is read ﴿*turjaʿūn*﴾ with an open *tā'* [[Zamakhshari's words "read *turjaʿūn* with an open *tā'*": al-Nasafi's wording is "with an open *tā'* and a kasra on the *jīm*." (ʿ)]].

﴿*al-Ḥaqq*﴾ ("the True"): the One to whom sovereignty is due, because everything is from Him and returns to Him. Or: the Established, who does not cease, and whose dominion does not cease.

The Throne is described as ﴿*al-Karīm*﴾ ("Noble") because mercy, good and blessing descend from it. Or because of its relation to the Most Noble of the noble, as one says "a noble house" when its inhabitants are noble. It is also read ﴿*al-Karīmu*﴾ with a *ḍamma* (nominative). Similar to it is ﴿*dhū l-ʿarshi l-majīd*﴾ ("Lord of the Throne, the Glorious").

﴿*lā burhāna lahu bihi*﴾ ("he has no proof for it") is like His saying ﴿*mā lam yunazzil bihi sulṭānan*﴾ ("for which He has sent down no authority"). It is a necessary descriptive phrase, like His saying ﴿*yaṭīru bi-janāḥayhi*﴾ ("flying with its two wings"). It is brought for emphasis, not to imply that among the gods there is anything for which a proof could stand. It is also permissible for it to be a parenthetical statement between the condition and its response, as when you say: "Whoever does good to Zayd—none is more deserving of good than him—then God will reward him."

It is read ﴿*annahu lā yufliḥu*﴾ with an open *hamza*. Its meaning: his reckoning is the non-success (of the disbeliever). The original is: his reckoning is that he himself does not succeed. ﴿*al-kāfirūn*﴾ ("the disbelievers") was put in place of the pronoun, because ﴿*man yadʿu*﴾ ("whoever calls upon") has the sense of the plural.
